title: The stopping days
hookLine: Friday prayers, Shabbat, Sunday, Buddhist observance days: many traditions stop work on purpose
last: WHAT WAS LOST WAS HELD, NOT WHO YOU ARE.

cards: A Friday at midday, and a shopkeeper pulls down the shutter and walks toward the mosque. A Friday at sunset, and a family lights candles and the phones go into a drawer.

A Sunday morning, and church bells over quiet streets. A full-moon day, and a woman in white walks to a Buddhist temple to keep extra precepts until the next morning. Different calendars, different reasons.
But each is a stopping, chosen on purpose and kept together. Today: uposatha.

teach.b: Each tradition stops in its own way. First, Shabbat.
The Ten Commandments in Exodus say, "Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work."

Then the verse keeps going: not you, nor your son or daughter, nor your servants, nor your animals, nor the stranger within your gates. The rest is for everyone in the household, including those who work for you.
Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. Second, Friday in Islam.

The Qur'an tells believers, when the call to the Friday congregational prayer is heard, to hurry to the remembrance of God and leave their trading; and when the prayer is done, to go out and seek God's bounty again.
So Friday isn't a full day off; it's a stopping in the middle of the day, for prayer together. Third, Sunday.
The book of Revelation speaks of being "in the Spirit on the Lord's day," and Christian tradition came to read the Lord's day as Sunday, the day of the resurrection.

Some Christians keep it as a day of rest; others gather and then go about the day; and some, such as Seventh-day Adventists, keep the seventh day, Saturday. Fourth, Buddhist observance days, called uposatha.
In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha teaches lay followers to keep extra precepts on these days, for a night and a day, following the example of the awakened ones.
These days don't ask for the same thing. What they share is a refusal to let work fill every hour.

how: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; Muslims gather for the Friday congregational prayer at midday; Christians commonly gather on Sunday, and some keep it as a day of rest; Buddhist lay followers may keep extra precepts on uposatha days.

practice: Let your hands fall still, and if something in you is still working, planning, answering, let it hear the shutter come down.
Then gently look ahead at your week for an afternoon, an evening or a morning that could become a stopping time, kept on purpose. Don't schedule it yet; just find it, and imagine the quiet in it.
